research_concepts: defensive suppression of opponent H2-H1 change
regression to the mean and mechanical coupling of H1 and H2-H1
methodological_questions: Is between-defense variance in opponent H2-H1 change larger than game-level noise (ICC or split-half reliability)?
Does the trait persist across adjacent seasons for the same team?
How much of the H2-H1 change is mechanical, from H1 level, score state and substitution patterns?

historical_evidence.finding: Season stability of each star's top sequential suppressor: only 2/30 (7%) met the 75% same-top-suppressor stability rule (30 stars x 4 seasons, min n=20/cell). Recorded as an adequately powered null.
Split-half stability of a usage-residual player influence measure was high (pooled rho about +0.67 to +0.69). This is a player-level offensive-structure measure, not a defensive H2-H1 effect.
Team offensive association structure is more similar to itself across split halves than to other teams (Frobenius S about 0.35, p<0.01). This is offensive structure, not defensive suppression.

Inferred defensive scheme-change labels showed change in 99% of units with near-uniform transition matrices. The record's caveat is that inferred labels cannot separate real defensive adjustment from the offense executing differently, which is consistent with label noise.

An apparent adapter PPP lift failed falsification: wrong-way teams did not do worse than no-signal teams, there was no carryover to the next game, and selection and regression to the mean were flagged.
Series-level AVOID share vs winning was inconclusive (rho=-0.26, p=0.07, n=50). It was confounded by team quality, and about 80 series were needed.
Team AVOID% varies widely (6.8% to 50.6%) in descriptive trigger-game tables, with no outcome test.
Descriptive regular-season vs playoff PPP allowed by play type for 25 teams, with no inferential test and a possible tagging-difference caveat.
Teammate play-type similarity did not separate absorption from cascade (wrong-signed rho=-0.19). Recorded failure type is a powered null with label error.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Season-over-season stability of individually identified suppressor patterns (top suppressor per star)
Inferring defensive scheme or adjustment labels from play-type sequences
failed_approaches.why: Label noise; cannot separate defensive adjustment from offensive execution.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Treating a PPP change after a coverage-response signal as real adaptation
failed_approaches.why: Construction, selection and regression-to-the-mean artifact; no carryover.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Series-level tests of counter-strategy share against winning

evidence_establishes: No retrieved record directly tests whether a defense's effect on opponent H2-H1 change is a reliable team trait.
Related project work shows that reliability claims about defensive or suppressor patterns have failed when the unit was fine-grained (FAM:SF-APPA-058, recorded as rejected).
Related project work shows that inferred defensive-adjustment labels and H1-to-H2 style changes are prone to label noise and artifact (FAM:SF-APPA-005, FAM:SF-APPA-001).
Split-half reliability is an established method in this project, with positive results for offensive and player-level measures (FAM:SF17, FAM:SF18).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether team-level defensive H2-H1 suppression has non-zero true between-team variance.
Whether any such trait persists across seasons.
Anything about H2-H1 scoring or efficiency specifically, since no retrieved record used that outcome.
Anything about effects that survive adjustment for game state.
own_inferences: Opponent H2-H1 change per game is very noisy (game-level SD likely around 10-15 points, so a team-season mean over about 82 games has SE near 1.5 points), while true between-defense differences are probably small. I expect low reliability.

H2-H1 change is mechanically coupled to H1 level, because a very strong H1 defense gives a positive expected H2-H1 change by regression to the mean. It is also coupled to game score through garbage time, starter rest and pace. A naive trait will largely capture defensive quality or score-state effects.
The word 'effect' is causal. Only a reliable, adjusted trait (a descriptive claim) is testable here, not a causal effect of the defense.
Team-level pooling (120 team-seasons) gives much better power than the failed player-level fine-grained tests, but is still limited for season-to-season correlations (90 adjacent pairs).
uncertainties: The size of true between-team variance is unknown, so the power calculation is a guess.
It is unclear whether the H2-H1 outcome should be points, PPP, or possession-based, and how garbage time should be defined.
Coaching and roster changes between seasons may reduce year-to-year persistence even if within-season reliability exists.
Playoff data are sparse per team and mixed in quality of opposition.
The retrieval returned no directly matching record, so relevance of the analogous evidence is limited.

historical_effect.explanation: The retrieved records did not answer the question, but SF-APPA-058 (rejected), SF-APPA-005 (untestable) and SF-APPA-001 (artifact) moved me from a plain proceed to proceed_with_changes. I added a pre-specified adjustment for H1 level and game state, a split-half or ICC check before any season-to-season claim, and a null-calibrating permutation and placebo. I also lowered the probability of a supported result.

blocking_constraints.text: Only 120 team-seasons (30 teams x 4 seasons) and about 90 adjacent-season pairs. A modest true reliability (ICC below about 0.05) cannot be distinguished from zero.
Per-game H2-H1 change has a huge noise-to-signal ratio, so the reliability ceiling is low by construction.

prior_work.summary: No retrieved record tests defensive H2-H1 suppression as a team trait. Adjacent work argues for caution: a stability null at the suppressor level, label-noise and artifact problems for adjustment constructs, and positive split-half precedent only for offensive or player-level measures.

risks.text: The H2-H1 change is mechanically negatively correlated with H1 level. Strong defenses show positive changes, so a 'trait' could reflect defensive quality or RTM.
Garbage time, score state, rest, opponent offense quality, injuries, home/away, and opponent's own H2-H1 tendencies (offensive fatigue, bench usage) all affect the outcome.
Game-level noise dominates; reliability estimates are attenuated and have wide confidence intervals.
30 teams per season; 90 year-to-year pairs; a CI on the reliability will be wide.
Rosters, coaching staffs and league scoring environment change across 2022-23 to 2025-26, which reduces year-to-year persistence independently of within-season reliability.
Multiple outcome definitions (points, PPP, eFG), garbage-time thresholds and split schemes create forking paths.
Season-level adjustments (team quality, opponent baseline) computed from the same games used for the reliability test would leak. Use out-of-sample baselines.
Half boundaries, overtime, and period-clock handling in play-by-play could misassign possessions.

design.estimand: Between-defense variance in the adjusted opponent H2-H1 change in points per 100 possessions: (a) within-season split-half reliability, as the Spearman-Brown corrected correlation of team means across random odd/even game splits, together with the ICC from a mixed model with a defense random intercept; (b) year-to-year persistence, as the correlation of team-season random effects across adjacent seasons for the same franchise. The trait is a descriptive property, not a causal effect.
design.unit: Team-season (defense), with games as repeated measures. Outcome per game is the opponent's H2 minus H1 points per 100 possessions.
design.sample: Regular seasons 2022-23 through 2025-26 (all complete as of 2026-10-06). 30 teams x 4 seasons = 120 team-seasons; 90 adjacent pairs. Primary analysis excludes playoffs (sparse). Exclude overtime from H2 and report a sensitivity analysis excluding games with a H1-end margin beyond a pre-set threshold (for example, 20 points) or garbage-time possessions.
design.power: Simulation-based power analysis before looking at outcomes, using the observed per-game SD and about 82 games per team-season. State the minimum detectable ICC (likely about 0.03-0.05 for the within-season test) and the minimum detectable year-to-year r (about 0.29 for n=90 at 80% power). If the minimum detectable value exceeds a practically meaningful reliability (for example, 0.3 for team means), report the study as underpowered rather than as a null.
design.controls: Include in the mixed model: opponent offense random effect and opponent's season-average H2-H1 change, H1-end score margin, home/away, rest days, back-to-back, pace, defense's own H1 efficiency (to handle RTM), and a spline of H1 level. Use out-of-sample (leave-one-game-out or split-based) baselines to avoid leakage. Compute the split-half within season using random game splits and also chronological splits.
design.falsification: (1) Permutation null: shuffle defense labels within opponent and season to get the null ICC and reliability distribution. (2) Placebo outcome: reliability of defense effect on a non-H2-H1 control (for example, H1-only efficiency) should be high if the measure works, while reliability of a within-half random split (first-quarter vs second-quarter) should be near zero. (3) Compare against the reliability implied by H1 defensive quality alone; the trait counts only if it adds beyond it. (4) Mechanical-floor check: simulate games with team-constant defense and no H2-specific effect to see the reliability produced by RTM alone.
design.multiplicity: Pre-register one primary outcome (points per 100 possessions, garbage time excluded by pre-stated rule) and one primary test per estimand (within-season ICC, year-to-year r). Treat other outcomes and thresholds as secondary with Holm-Bonferroni correction; report all forks.
design.decision_rule: Supported only if the adjusted within-season split-half reliability has a lower 95% CI bound above 0 and above the permutation 95th percentile, and the year-to-year correlation is positive with its CI excluding 0 after H1-level adjustment. Rejected if the upper CI bounds fall below the pre-set smallest meaningful reliability (ICC of 0.05, year-to-year r of 0.2) and the minimum detectable effect is adequate. Otherwise report as inconclusive or underpowered. Any result that vanishes after H1-level adjustment is labelled an RTM artifact.
design.data_version: NBA stats API per-game play-by-play and box-score files, regular seasons 2022-23 through 2025-26, snapshot frozen as of 2026-10-06. Pre-register code and parameters before any outcome is inspected.

methodological_questions: Is a defense's effect on opponents' H2-H1 change stable across seasons or split-halves of games?
How much of opponent H2-H1 change is noise, regression to the mean, or confounded by game score and garbage time?
What sample size and reliability are available with 120 team-seasons?

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- explore_graph(node_id): the relationships of one graph node (a family or a question, method, dataset, measure, limitation or risk node), with neighbour labels.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

reasoning_details.text:
I'm weighing whether more tool calls are needed, and concluding I could wrap up now. The retrieved records don't directly address defensive suppression reliability, though a few related ones (on season stability and split-half persistence) turn up, with mixed support.

I'm sketching the design for the analysis now: 30 teams over four seasons, estimating each defense's effect on opponents' second-half-minus-first-half change. For reliability I'd check split-half and year-to-year consistency, but with per-game noise this large, the true team-level variance probably looks small, so I expect low reliability.

I'm laying out the reliability checks: split-half and year-to-year consistency across the 30 teams. I also need to handle the fact that opponent H2-H1 change partly reflects the team's own first-half results through regression to the mean, so I'm leaning toward a definition that avoids that. Given the noise, I expect low reliability, but I'm not sure whether the sample is large enough to detect even a small true effect.

I'm noting the data is frozen as of October 6, 2026, with the 2025-26 season complete, and I'm setting aside the playoffs from the main analysis since they're a small sample.
